author: Jane Austen
fact_sheet_sources: Wikipedia: Pride and Prejudice, George Wickham, Georgiana Darcy, Lady Catherine de Bourgh, Mr William Collins

key_facts.publication: Published 1813; originally written as First Impressions (1796-97)
key_facts.author: Jane Austen (1775-1817), daughter of a country clergyman
key_facts.setting: Longbourn (Bennet home, Hertfordshire), Netherfield (Bingley's leased estate), Hunsford (Collins's parsonage, Kent), Rosings (Lady Catherine's estate, Kent), Pemberley (Darcy's estate, Derbyshire)
key_facts.bennet_sisters: Jane (eldest), Elizabeth (second), Mary, Kitty/Catherine, Lydia (youngest). Lydia is 15 at start, 16 at elopement.
key_facts.incomes: Darcy: £10,000/year. Bingley: 'four or five thousand a year' (not a fixed sum). Wickham received £3,000 in lieu of the Kympton living.
key_facts.wickham_settlement: Darcy paid Wickham's debts (more than £1,000), an additional £1,000 added to Lydia's dowry, and purchased Wickham's army commission. Total approx £3,000 — NOT £10,000 (Mr Bennet's speculation only).

proposals.darcy_first: Chapter 34, at Hunsford parsonage. Opens with 'In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.'
proposals.darcy_second: Chapter 58, during an outdoor walk near Longbourn. Opens with 'You are too generous to trifle with me. If your feelings are still what they were last April, tell me so at once.'

key_quote_attributions.against_my_will: Elizabeth's paraphrase of Darcy's proposal in her rebuttal (Ch. 34): 'why... you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character' — these are ELIZABETH'S words characterising Darcy, NOT Darcy's direct speech
key_quote_attributions.in_vain_have_i_struggled: Darcy, Ch. 34. Correct: 'In vain HAVE I struggled' (inverted order). 'In vain I have struggled' is the film-adaptation variant.
key_quote_attributions.tolerable_but_not_handsome: Darcy, Ch. 3, at the Meryton assembly
key_quote_attributions.how_despicably_i_have_acted: Elizabeth, Ch. 36, after reading Darcy's letter
key_quote_attributions.i_was_in_the_middle: Darcy, Ch. 60 (after engagement, not at Pemberley)

key_facts.marriages: Four marriages: Charlotte/Collins (Ch. 22), Lydia/Wickham (forced by Darcy's intervention, Ch. 52), Jane/Bingley (Ch. 55), Elizabeth/Darcy (Ch. 58). Charlotte/Collins is not part of the final resolution.
key_facts.pemberley_chapters: Ch. 42 (travel/decision), Ch. 43 (visit and unexpected Darcy encounter), Ch. 44 (Darcy and Georgiana call on Elizabeth). 'Chapters 42-43' covers the core visit; 'Chapters 42-44' covers the full Pemberley episode.
key_facts.darcy_letter: Chapter 35, delivered morning after first proposal

issues.description: Misattributes 'against my will, against my reason, and even against my character' as Darcy's direct speech to Elizabeth in his proposal. The text says: 'He tells Elizabeth he loves her "against my will, against my reason, and even against my character."' In fact, these are Elizabeth's words in her rebuttal (Ch. 34), paraphrasing and characterising Darcy's proposal back at him. Darcy's actual opening is 'In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed.'
issues.source: P&P Ch. 34, pemberley.com/etext/PandP/chapter34.htm: Elizabeth says 'why... you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character?'

issues.description: Two errors: (1) 'The novel ends with three marriages' — the novel in fact contains four marriages: Charlotte/Collins (Ch. 22), Lydia/Wickham, Jane/Bingley, and Elizabeth/Darcy. The Charlotte/Collins marriage is omitted from the count. (2) 'Comparing the Two Proposals: The first proposal is a catalogue of Darcy's pride: "against my will, against my reason, and even against my character"' — same misattribution as PNP-001: these are Elizabeth's words describing Darcy's proposal, not his direct speech.
issues.source: P&P: four marriages confirmed in novel. Charlotte accepts Collins in Ch. 22. 'Against my will' is Elizabeth's characterisation in Ch. 34, not Darcy's direct quote.

issues.description: 'Three marriages resolve the novel: Elizabeth and Darcy... Jane and Bingley... and Lydia and Wickham.' This framing omits Charlotte and Collins's marriage, which is part of the novel's four-marriage structural commentary. While Charlotte/Collins married earlier and not in the resolution chapters, stating only 'three marriages resolve the novel' without contextualising that a fourth (Charlotte/Collins) also exists risks students thinking there are only three marriages in the whole novel.
issues.source: P&P contains four marriages. Charlotte and Collins marry in Ch. 22, not in the resolution but as part of Austen's broader marriage commentary.

issues.description: Quotes Darcy's first proposal opening as 'In vain I have struggled' — the word order is incorrect. The original Austen text is 'In vain have I struggled' (inverted auxiliary). 'In vain I have struggled' is the phrasing used in some film adaptations (not the novel text).
issues.source: P&P Ch. 34 full text: 'In vain have I struggled.' Confirmed at pemberley.com/etext/PandP/chapter34.htm and Goodreads/authoritative sources.

issues.description: Places Darcy's quote 'I was in the middle before I knew that I had begun' in the context of the Pemberley visit section. This quote is actually spoken in Chapter 60 (after the engagement), not during or immediately after the Pemberley episode. The lesson uses it as evidence of Darcy's acknowledgement during the Pemberley arc, but it strictly belongs to the post-engagement conversation. Minor contextual displacement.
issues.source: P&P Ch. 60: Darcy says this when Elizabeth asks when he fell in love, well after the Pemberley visit.

issues.description: 'Mr and Mrs Bennet: he married for beauty, she for security' — Mr Bennet's motivation (beauty) is directly stated in the novel (Ch. 42 and 50 narrator commentary). However, Mrs Bennet's motivation as 'security' is an inference/interpretation, not an explicit statement in the text. The novel focuses almost entirely on Mr Bennet's perspective on their marriage. This is a reasonable interpretive claim common in criticism, but presenting it as a paired fact alongside the textually explicit 'beauty' claim could mislead students into thinking both are equally text-based.
issues.source: P&P Ch. 42: 'captivation of youth and beauty' is explicit for Mr Bennet. Mrs Bennet's motivation is not stated by the narrator; the 'security' claim is interpretive.

issues.description: Describes Wickham as eloping with 'fifteen-year-old Lydia'. Lydia is 15 at the start of the novel but turns 16 before the elopement (her birthday is in June; the elopement is in summer/July). The text at the news of the elopement refers to Lydia as 16. This is a minor but technically inaccurate age claim.
issues.source: Lydia Bennet wiki and novel timeline: Lydia born June, elopement in summer (likely July), making her 16 at time of elopement. Ch. 47 context and Lydia Bennet's letter confirms she is described elsewhere as 16.

issues.description: States Elizabeth's visit to Pemberley is in 'Chapters 42-43'. The decision to visit is in Ch. 42; the actual visit and encounter with Darcy is in Ch. 43. The follow-up (Darcy and Georgiana calling on Elizabeth) is Ch. 44. 'Chapters 42-43' captures the core event but omits Ch. 44, which is part of the Pemberley episode. This is a minor omission, not incorrect.
issues.source: SparkNotes and CliffsNotes: Ch. 43 = visit, Ch. 44 = Darcy and Georgiana's return call on Elizabeth at Lambton.

notes: The most significant error (PNP-001, PNP-002) is the misattribution of 'against my will, against my reason, and even against my character' as Darcy's direct speech. This phrase is Elizabeth's paraphrase of Darcy's proposal in her rebuttal, not Darcy's own words.

The 'three marriages' framing in AQA and OCR Resolution lessons omits Charlotte and Collins (Charlotte/Collins marry in Ch. 22, not the final resolution). Students taught this could incorrectly believe there are only three marriages in the novel.
The OCR quote 'In vain I have struggled' uses film-adaptation word order rather than Austen's original 'In vain have I struggled'.
All facts about financial figures (Darcy £10,000/year, Bingley 'four or five thousand', Georgiana £30,000, Wickham £3,000) are correctly rendered across all boards.
Chapter attributions for all proposals and the Lady Catherine confrontation are accurate across all boards.
The Eduqas and Edexcel boards are cleanest — no high or medium severity issues.
